diagnostic_evidence.quote: It follows from the fact that $\mathcal{B}_1$ is continuously embedded into $H^1(\Omega)$, and $H^1(\Omega)$ is compactly embedded into $L^2(\Omega)$.

issues.failure_explanation: A continuous embedding B_1 into H^1 followed by the compact embedding H^1 into L^2 yields only L^2-convergent subsequences (and weak H^1 convergence). It does not yield strong H^1 convergence. The strong H^1 compactness of B_1-balls would need a separate argument, such as compactness of the closed convex hull of the ridge functions, and none is given.

failure_location.quote: Any bounded sequence in Barron space $\mathcal{B}_1$ has a subsequence that converges in $H^1(\Omega)$

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Either prove H^1-relative compactness of bounded subsets of B_1 (e.g. via Mazur's theorem applied to the closed convex hull of the compact family of normalized ReLU ridge functions), or weaken the lemma and the dependent conclusions to L^2 convergence.
issues.overall_effect: The H^1(Ω) convergence of Algorithm 1 in Theorem 1, and of Algorithm 2 for R=R_2 in Theorem 2, rests on this lemma. The contradiction argument in the proof of Theorem 1 uses H^1-convergence of the subsequence to contradict ||f-f†||_{H^1}≥ε. These H^1 conclusions are unsupported as written.
issues.title: Lemma claims H^1-compactness of Barron balls but the proof only gives L^2-compactness
issues.why_classification: A contained new argument, or a limited weakening to L^2 convergence, repairs it without changing the overall architecture.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Let $r:=r(n)$ be a monotonic increasing function

issues.failure_explanation: The proof needs the comparison network f_n to lie in X_{n,r(n)}, i.e. r(n)≥c_ρ(f†) for large n, and it justifies this by 'the definition of r(n)'. No such definition exists: r is only monotonic increasing and may be bounded below c_ρ(f†). Theorem 2 states no condition on r, and the prose says none is needed, so the hypothesis is omitted although the proof requires it.

failure_location.quote: by the definition of $r(n)$, we have $r(n)\to +\infty$

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Add the hypothesis r(n)→∞ (or r(n)≥c_ρ(f†) for large n) to Theorem 2 and correct the accompanying prose. This needs no knowledge of c_ρ(f†) beyond r(n)→∞.
issues.overall_effect: Termination and the bounds on n(δ) and k(δ), and the convergence claims, are unsupported for general r(n). The advertised absence of conditions on r(n) is incorrect.
issues.title: Theorem 2 needs r(n)→∞ (or r(n)≥c_ρ(f†) eventually), which is neither assumed nor derivable
issues.why_classification: Adding a standard local hypothesis preserves the method, rates and the no-prior-knowledge scope.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Combining these with the bound $b(k^*) \le C_b b(k^*-1) \le C_b N$

issues.failure_explanation: The stopping size satisfies n(δ)≤b(k*) with b(k*)>N, so n(δ)≤N does not follow. Only n(δ)≤C_b N holds. The uniform bound on δ n(δ)^{θ/2}, and hence the bound on the H^1 norm and B_1 norm of the iterates, is therefore derived with an invalid inequality.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Use n(δ)≤C_b N and correct the constants (δ n(δ)^{θ/2}≤(C_b C_max)^{θ/2}).
issues.overall_effect: The boundedness constants in the convergence part of Theorem 2 are not justified as written. The conclusions survive after replacing C_max by C_b C_max.
issues.title: Proof of Theorem 2 uses n(δ)≤N although only n(δ)≤b(k*)≤C_b N is shown
issues.why_classification: The fix is a local constant adjustment and the conclusions are unchanged.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Hence, by the monotonicity of $\varphi$ and the definition of its generalized inverse $\varphi^{-1}$ as in \eqref{gInv}, we obtain

issues.failure_explanation: Parts (a) and (b) need a uniform bound on c_{ρ_n}(f) from φ(c)≤const. This requires φ to be strictly increasing and unbounded, so that φ(c)≤y gives c≤φ^{-1}(y)<∞. Assumption (A2) only gives 'continuous increasing', so a bounded or flat φ makes the bound fail and minimizers may not exist in X_{n,∞}. The proof also writes P(f)≤T_α(f,g), ignoring the factor α (it should be αP≤T_α). In (b) it writes φ(||f||_{B_1})=P(f), where only ≤ holds, and then treats a B_1 bound as membership in X_{n,R}, which needs a bound on c_{ρ_n}.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Assume φ is strictly increasing with φ(t)→∞, bound c_{ρ_n} via αφ(c)≤T_α, and work with c_{ρ_n} instead of ||·||_{B_1} when placing iterates in X_{n,R}. The paper's choice φ(t)=t^2 satisfies this.
issues.overall_effect: Existence and stability are not established for the stated class of φ. Later results that use these bounds and the generalized inverse φ^{-1} are affected.
issues.title: Existence/stability proof needs coercivity of φ and mishandles α
issues.why_classification: A standard local hypothesis plus routine corrections suffice, and all results hold for the intended φ.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Finally, using the monotonicity of $\varphi$ and the choice of probability $\rho$, and passing to the limit $n,\ell\to\infty$ in \eqref{eqvarphi}, we obtain

issues.failure_explanation: The bound from (b) holds for fixed n with a constant R_n^1 that depends on n. In (c) n→∞, so a bound uniform in n is needed. This is only obtained later from (eqvarphi), which makes the compactness step circular. The proof also asserts f†∈B_1 and ||f†||_{B_1}≤liminf||f_{n,k}||_{B_1} for an L^2-limit without proof. Proposition 2 gives only a normed space, with no completeness or lower semicontinuity of the Barron norm under L^2 convergence. These are needed to conclude R(f†)≤R(f̄).

failure_location.quote: By (b), the family $\{f_{n,k}\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}}$ is bounded in $\mathcal{B}_1$ and hence relatively compact in $L^2(\Omega)$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Reorder the argument to use the uniform bound from (eqvarphi). Add a lemma, or a citation, that bounded B_1 sets are L^2-precompact with B_1-closed limits and that the B_1 norm is lower semicontinuous under L^2 convergence.
issues.overall_effect: The claim that the limit is an R-minimizing solution in B_1 is not rigorously established. Theorem 4 and Corollary 1 use it.
issues.title: Convergence part (c) omits closedness/lower semicontinuity of the B_1 norm and uses a fixed-n bound
issues.why_classification: A contained new lemma and a reordering repair it while keeping the theorem's content.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: An a priori scale that balances the two terms in

issues.failure_explanation: For a concave sublinear index function such as Φ(t)=c t^μ with μ<1, sup_{t≥0}{αt-Φ(t)} equals +∞ for every α>0, so Φ^* and its inverse are meaningless. The Young inequality actually needed involves the conjugate of the convex function Φ^{-1}. The statement's third term also lacks the factor α^{-1} that the proof produces after dividing by α. The claim that α≍δ/Φ(τδ) balances the terms is asserted without verification.

failure_location.quote: $\Phi^{-*}$ denotes the (generalized) inverse of the Fenchel conjugate $\Phi^*$ of $\Phi$, defined by $\Phi^*(\alpha) := \sup_{t \ge 0} \{\alpha t - \Phi(t)\}$

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Redefine the term via the conjugate of Φ^{-1}, restore the α^{-1} factor, and add a short argument that this term is O(δ/α) for α≍δ/Φ(τδ), using concavity of Φ.
issues.overall_effect: Estimate (errorestimate) and the general rate in (ii) are not correctly formulated or proved for general Φ. The explicit power-law case can be checked directly.
issues.title: Φ^{-*} is ill-defined for concave index functions and the error estimate is inconsistent with its proof
issues.why_classification: A contained redefinition and a short lemma repair it, leaving a comparable result.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: According to Theorem~\ref{well-posedness}(c), we have $f_{n,\alpha}^{\delta}\to f^{\dagger}$ in $L^2(\Omega)$ as $\delta\to0$ and $n\to\infty$

issues.failure_explanation: Theorem 3(c) gives L^2 convergence only when α→0 and α^{-1}(δ+n^{-s/2})→0. The proof of Theorem 4 invokes it to place f_{n,α}^δ in the ε-ball where the variational source condition holds. The statement itself imposes no condition tying α to δ and n, so for arbitrary small α,δ, n the convergence claim and the application of the source condition are unjustified.

failure_location.quote: (i) for any sufficient small $\alpha,\delta$, we have

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Add the condition α→0, α^{-1}(δ+n^{-s/2})→0 to the hypotheses of Theorem 4(i).
issues.overall_effect: Convergence and estimate (i) are valid only under the Theorem 3(c) parameter choice. The specific choices in (ii) satisfy it.
issues.title: Theorem 4 asserts convergence and the estimate for 'any' small α,δ without the parameter-coupling condition
issues.why_classification: Adding the condition used in the proof repairs it, and the rate statements in (ii) already satisfy it.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: the auto-convolution operator is not injective (e.g.\ $A(f)=A(-f)$)
However, when restricted to the cone of strictly nonnegative functions (e.g.\ $f\in C[0,1]$ with $f>0$),

issues.failure_explanation: Theorems 1 and 2 conclude f*=f† from injectivity of A on the space containing limits of the algorithm's iterates. The algorithms minimize over X_{n,r(n)}, which contains sign-changing ReLU networks, and A(-f†)=A(f†)=g. Injectivity on the positive cone therefore does not give the required hypothesis, and a minimizing sequence may converge to -f†. The positivity constraint is never imposed on the networks, and the approximation theorem does not guarantee nonnegative approximants.

failure_location.quote: Thus, $A$ is locally Lipschitz at any $f^\dagger\in H^1(\Omega)$, and Example~\ref{Ex2} meets the assumptions of Theorems~1-2.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Weaken the claim to illustrative use, or constrain the networks to a nonnegative class and supply a nonnegative approximation result.
issues.overall_effect: The theory does not cover Example 2 as implemented, so the example does not validate the theorems for this nonlinear operator.
issues.title: Example 2 is claimed to satisfy the injectivity hypotheses although the networks are unconstrained in sign
issues.why_classification: Honest weakening is easy, but keeping the claim needs a new constrained-class approximation argument.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Moreover, we quantify the network size required to realize this rate
This result theoretically confirms that a larger network is not always beneficial.

issues.failure_explanation: Theorems 1, 2 and 4 give only upper bounds or sufficient choices n(δ)=O(δ^{-2/θ}) and n≍δ^{-2/s}. There is no lower bound and no result that a smaller or larger n fails to achieve the rate, or that larger networks degrade stability. Optimality of the size (Q4) and the theoretical confirmation of non-benefit of large networks (Q2) are therefore not established. The latter is only empirical.

failure_location.quote: imply an optimal choice for the number of neurons

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Reword to 'sufficient' network size and present the non-monotonic error behavior as numerical observation, or prove matching lower bounds.
issues.overall_effect: The stated answers to Q2 and Q4, and the abstract's claim about overfitting with larger architectures, overstate what is proved.
issues.title: Claims of an 'optimal' network size and of theoretically confirmed non-benefit of larger networks are unsupported
issues.why_classification: Rewording the claims repairs it and leaves the theorems unchanged.
